title: stockflow: warehouse inventory, costing and replenishment utilities
description: Shared helpers used by the fulfilment, purchasing and finance teams to work with warehouse stock data: SKU and bin-location parsing, movement-record processing, on-hand and cycle-count reporting, inventory costing (FIFO, weighted average, freight allocation), replenishment planning and parcel building. Quantities are integer eaches, money is integer cents and dates are integer day indices, so every service computes the same numbers.

functions.signature: def normalize_sku(code: str) -> str:
functions.summary: Validate SKU codes (with check digit) and return the canonical form
functions.spec:
Validate a SKU code and return it in canonical form.

Canonical SKUs look like "ABC-123456-1": a three-letter category prefix
(A-Z), a hyphen, a six-digit item number, a hyphen and one check digit.
Input may use any letter case and may carry surrounding whitespace.

Check digit: weight the six item digits 3,1,3,1,3,1 from left to right,
sum the products and take (10 - sum % 10) % 10.

Args:
    code: SKU as typed or scanned.

Returns:
    The canonical, upper-case SKU string.

Raises:
    ValueError: if the code is malformed or the check digit is wrong.

Examples:
    normalize_sku(" abc-123456-1 ") == "ABC-123456-1"
    normalize_sku("ABC-123456-2")   -> ValueError (check digit should be 1)
functions.clarification:
Older shelf labels and supplier ASN files print SKUs without the hyphens,
e.g. "ABC1234561". That compact form must be accepted too and normalized to the
hyphenated form ("ABC-123456-1"). A code has either both hyphens or none; a code
with only one of the two hyphens is malformed.

functions.signature: def parse_location(code: str) -> Tuple[str, int, int, int]:
functions.summary: Parse bin location codes into zone, aisle, shelf and level
functions.spec:
Parse a warehouse bin location code.

Location codes have the form "Z-AA-SS-L": a zone letter, a two-digit aisle
number, a two-digit shelf (bay) number and a one-digit level, separated by
hyphens, e.g. "B-07-14-3" (zone B, aisle 7, shelf 14, level 3).
Letter case and surrounding whitespace are ignored.

Returns:
    (zone, aisle, shelf, level) with the zone upper-cased and the numbers as ints.

Raises:
    ValueError: if the code does not follow the format.

Example:
    parse_location("b-07-14-3") == ("B", 7, 14, 3)
functions.clarification:
Aisles and shelves are numbered from 01: "00" does not exist for either of
them and must be rejected with ValueError. Level 0 is valid (it is the floor
position under the first beam).

functions.signature: def parse_quantity(text: str, case_size: int) -> int:
functions.summary: Convert quantity strings like '5 CS' to eaches
functions.spec:
Convert a quantity string such as "5 CS" or "-3 ea" to eaches.

Format: an optional sign, an integer, optional whitespace and a unit of
measure. Supported units (case-insensitive):
    EA   each, 1 unit
    CS   case, `case_size` units
Surrounding whitespace is ignored.

Args:
    text: quantity as printed on the movement record.
    case_size: eaches per case for the SKU, must be >= 1.

Raises:
    ValueError: malformed text, unknown unit, or case_size < 1.

Examples:
    parse_quantity("5 CS", 12) == 60
    parse_quantity("-3ea", 12) == -3
functions.clarification:
Some older scanner feeds send only the number, without a unit ("12" or
"-4"). A bare number is a quantity in eaches and must be accepted, not rejected.

functions.signature: def round_to_pack(qty: int, pack_size: int, min_packs: int = 1) -> int:
functions.summary: Round order quantities to whole supplier packs
functions.spec:
Round an order quantity (in eaches) to whole supplier packs.

The result is a multiple of `pack_size` and never less than
`min_packs * pack_size`.

Args:
    qty: desired quantity in eaches, >= 0.
    pack_size: eaches per supplier pack, >= 1.
    min_packs: minimum number of packs to order (default 1), >= 0.

Raises:
    ValueError: if qty < 0, pack_size < 1 or min_packs < 0.

Examples:
    round_to_pack(24, 12) == 24
    round_to_pack(0, 12) == 12      # minimum of one pack
functions.clarification:
Rounding is to the NEAREST whole pack, not always up: 13 with packs of 12
becomes 12. A remainder of exactly half a pack rounds up (18 -> 24). Purchasing
does not want every PO inflated by almost a full pack.

functions.signature: def weighted_average_cost(layers: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]) -> int:
functions.summary: Compute the weighted average unit cost of cost layers in cents
functions.spec:
Weighted average unit cost of a set of cost layers, in whole cents.

Each layer is (quantity, unit_cost_cents). The result is the total cost of
all layers divided by the total quantity, rounded to the nearest cent.
Layers with quantity 0 contribute nothing.

Raises:
    ValueError: if a quantity or cost is negative, or the total quantity is 0.

Example:
    weighted_average_cost([(10, 200), (30, 300)]) == 275
functions.clarification:
Rounding is half-up: an exact half cent goes up (100.5 -> 101), the same
way finance rounds on the stock ledger. Do not use round-half-to-even, and keep
the arithmetic in integers.

functions.signature: def safety_stock(daily_demand: Sequence[int], lead_times: Sequence[int]) -> int:
functions.summary: Compute safety stock with the max-max method
functions.spec:
Safety stock in units, using the max-max method:

    safety stock = max daily demand * max lead time
                   - average daily demand * average lead time

Args:
    daily_demand: units demanded per day over the history window.
    lead_times: observed supplier lead times in days.

Returns:
    Safety stock as an int number of units (never negative).

Raises:
    ValueError: if either sequence is empty or contains a negative value.

Example:
    safety_stock([10, 20, 30], [4, 6]) == 30 * 6 - 20 * 5 == 80
functions.clarification:
The averages are used unrounded (exact fractions) and only the final result
is converted to whole units, always rounding UP: 16.25 units of safety stock
becomes 17. Planning never rounds a buffer down.

functions.signature: def reorder_point(daily_demand: Sequence[int], lead_times: Sequence[int], review_period_days: int = 0) -> int:
functions.summary: Compute a SKU's reorder point from demand history and lead times
functions.spec:
Reorder point for a SKU: expected demand over the replenishment cycle plus
safety stock.

    cycle demand  = average daily demand * (average lead time + review_period_days),
                    rounded up to a whole unit
    reorder point = cycle demand + safety_stock(daily_demand, lead_times)

Args:
    daily_demand: units shipped per day, oldest day first.
    lead_times: observed supplier lead times in days.
    review_period_days: days between scheduled stock reviews (0 for
        continuous review).

Raises:
    ValueError: if review_period_days < 0, plus anything safety_stock raises.

Example:
    reorder_point([10, 20, 30], [4, 6]) == 20 * 5 + 80 == 180
functions.clarification:
Planning uses a rolling four-week window: only the most recent 28 entries of
daily_demand are used, both for the cycle demand and for the safety_stock call.
Shorter histories are used as they are.

functions.signature: def economic_order_quantity(annual_demand: int, order_cost_cents: int, holding_cost_cents: int, pack_size: int = 1) -> int:
functions.summary: Compute the economic order quantity rounded to supplier packs
functions.spec:
Economic order quantity (EOQ), rounded to supplier packs.

    raw EOQ = floor(sqrt(2 * annual_demand * order_cost_cents / holding_cost_cents))

computed with integer arithmetic, then rounded to whole packs with
round_to_pack(raw, pack_size).

Args:
    annual_demand: units per year, >= 0.
    order_cost_cents: fixed cost of placing one purchase order, >= 0.
    holding_cost_cents: cost of holding one unit for a year, > 0.
    pack_size: supplier pack size, >= 1.

Returns:
    Order quantity in eaches; 0 when annual_demand is 0.

Raises:
    ValueError: on negative demand or order cost, holding cost <= 0, or
        pack_size < 1.

Example:
    economic_order_quantity(1200, 5000, 300) == 200
functions.clarification:
Never suggest more than one year of demand: if the pack-rounded EOQ is larger
than annual_demand, return round_to_pack(annual_demand, pack_size) instead. This
matters for slow movers with high ordering costs.

functions.signature: def fifo_cogs(layers: Sequence[Tuple[int, int, int]], qty: int) -> Tuple[int, List[Tuple[int, int, int]]]:
functions.summary: Cost a shipment with FIFO cost layers and return the remaining layers
functions.spec:
Cost of goods sold for a shipment, using FIFO cost layers.

Args:
    layers: (receipt_day, qty, unit_cost_cents) tuples, in any order.
    qty: eaches shipped, >= 0.

Layers are consumed oldest receipt_day first; layers received on the same
day are consumed in list order. Shipping more than the layers hold is
allowed (the warehouse may ship ahead of a late receipt); every layer is
then used up.

Returns:
    (cost_cents, remaining_layers). remaining_layers lists the layers that
    still hold stock, oldest first, in the same tuple form; a partially used
    layer appears with its reduced qty. The input is not modified.

Raises:
    ValueError: if qty < 0, or if qty > 0 and there are no layers at all.

Example:
    fifo_cogs([(3, 5, 120), (1, 10, 100)], 12) == (1240, [(3, 3, 120)])
functions.clarification:
Units shipped beyond what the layers hold (the shortfall) are costed at the
unit cost of the most recent receipt: the layer with the latest receipt_day, or
the last such layer in list order if several share that day. The shortfall is
neither free nor an error; finance trues it up when the late receipt is booked.

functions.signature: def allocate_freight(freight_cents: int, line_values: Sequence[int]) -> List[int]:
functions.summary: Allocate inbound freight across receipt lines by value, to the exact cent
functions.spec:
Allocate an inbound freight charge across receipt lines in proportion to
line value (landed cost allocation).

Each line first gets floor(freight_cents * value / total_value). The cents
left over are then handed out one at a time to the lines with the largest
fractional remainder, so the shares always add up to freight_cents exactly.

Args:
    freight_cents: total freight charge, >= 0.
    line_values: value of each receipt line in cents, >= 0.

Returns:
    List of allocated cents, one per line, in the order of line_values.

Raises:
    ValueError: on negative inputs, or if freight_cents > 0 while every
        line value is 0 (nothing to allocate against).

Examples:
    allocate_freight(1000, [3000, 1000]) == [750, 250]
    allocate_freight(100, [1, 1, 1]) == [34, 33, 33]
functions.clarification:
When fractional remainders tie, the leftover cent goes to the line with the
larger value first (large lines absorb rounding with the smallest relative
error); only when the values are equal as well does the earlier line win.

functions.signature: def abc_classify(values: Mapping[str, int], a_pct: int = 80, b_pct: int = 95) -> Dict[str, str]:
functions.summary: Classify SKUs into A/B/C classes by cumulative value share
functions.spec:
ABC classification of SKUs by value share.

SKUs are ranked by value, highest first (ties: SKU ascending), and the
running total of value is tracked as a share of the grand total. The top
SKUs making up the first `a_pct` percent of value are class "A", those up
to `b_pct` percent are "B", the rest are "C".

Args:
    values: SKU -> value in cents (e.g. annual consumption value).
    a_pct, b_pct: cumulative percentage thresholds, 0 < a_pct <= b_pct <= 100.

Returns:
    Dict SKU -> "A" | "B" | "C" for every SKU in `values`. SKUs with value 0
    are always "C" (so is every SKU when the total is 0).

Raises:
    ValueError: if a value is negative or the thresholds are invalid.

Example:
    abc_classify({"S1": 80, "S2": 15, "S3": 5}) == {"S1": "A", "S2": "B", "S3": "C"}
functions.clarification:
The SKU that crosses a threshold belongs to the higher class. A SKU is "A"
if the cumulative share BEFORE adding it is still below a_pct, and "B" if that
share is below b_pct. Example: values 50/40/10 give A, A, B (the second SKU takes
the running share from 50% to 90%, but it started below 80%).

functions.signature: def select_lots_fefo(lots: Sequence[Tuple[str, int, int]], qty: int, today: int, min_shelf_days: int = 0) -> List[Tuple[str, int]]:
functions.summary: Pick lots first-expired-first-out, honouring minimum shelf life
functions.spec:
Choose which lots to pick from, first-expired-first-out (FEFO).

Args:
    lots: (lot_id, expiry_day, available_qty) tuples for one SKU at one
        location. Days are integer day indices.
    qty: eaches to pick, >= 0.
    today: current day index.
    min_shelf_days: a lot is only eligible if it has at least this many days
        left until expiry (expiry_day - today >= min_shelf_days). Default 0.

Expired lots are never picked. Eligible lots are used in order of
expiry_day (earliest first), ties broken by lot_id ascending; each lot is
drained before moving on to the next one.

Returns:
    List of (lot_id, picked_qty) in picking order, containing only lots with
    picked_qty > 0.

Raises:
    ValueError: if qty < 0 or the eligible stock is less than qty.

Example:
    select_lots_fefo([("L2", 30, 5), ("L1", 20, 4)], 6, today=10)
        == [("L1", 4), ("L2", 2)]
functions.clarification:
expiry_day is the "best before" date printed on the case, and customers must
receive goods before that date, so a lot already counts as expired ON its
expiry_day: with min_shelf_days=0 a lot whose expiry_day == today is not
eligible. Expired therefore means expiry_day <= today.

functions.signature: def first_fit_decreasing(items: Sequence[Tuple[str, int]], capacity: int) -> List[List[Tuple[str, int]]]:
functions.summary: Pack weighted items into bins with first-fit-decreasing
functions.spec:
Pack weighted items into bins with the first-fit-decreasing heuristic.

Items are taken heaviest first. Each item goes into the first bin (in the
order the bins were opened) whose remaining capacity can hold it; if no bin
can, a new bin is opened.

Args:
    items: (item_id, weight) pairs; weights are non-negative ints.
    capacity: capacity of every bin, > 0.

Returns:
    List of bins in the order they were opened; each bin is a list of the
    (item_id, weight) tuples in the order they were placed.

Raises:
    ValueError: if capacity <= 0, a weight is negative, or a single item is
        heavier than capacity.

Example:
    first_fit_decreasing([("a", 4), ("b", 7), ("c", 3)], 10)
        == [[("b", 7), ("c", 3)], [("a", 4)]]
functions.clarification:
Items of equal weight are taken in ascending item_id order, not in input
order. Packing must come out the same however the order lines happened to be
listed (the same order arrives sorted differently from the storefront and from
customer service).

functions.signature: def split_shipment(lines: Sequence[Tuple[str, int, int]], max_parcel_grams: int) -> List[Dict[str, int]]:
functions.summary: Split an order into parcels under the carrier weight limit
functions.spec:
Split an order into parcels that respect the carrier's weight limit.

Args:
    lines: (sku, qty, unit_weight_grams) order lines. Lines with the same SKU
        are merged first (they must have the same unit weight).
    max_parcel_grams: carrier weight limit per parcel.

The goods are packed with first_fit_decreasing, using max_parcel_grams as
the bin capacity and the SKU as item id; a line may end up spread over
several parcels.

Returns:
    List of parcels in the order produced by first_fit_decreasing; each
    parcel is a dict SKU -> number of units in that parcel.

Raises:
    ValueError: if max_parcel_grams <= 0, a qty or unit weight is <= 0, a
        single unit is heavier than max_parcel_grams, or the same SKU appears
        with different unit weights.

Example:
    split_shipment([("TEE", 3, 400), ("MUG", 1, 700)], 1000)
        == [{"MUG": 1}, {"TEE": 2}, {"TEE": 1}]
functions.clarification:
Keep lines together when possible: a (merged) line whose total weight fits
within max_parcel_grams is packed as ONE item (weight qty x unit weight) and is
never split across parcels. Only lines heavier than the limit are broken into
single units. Customers kept complaining about getting one of two identical
items in a separate box.

functions.signature: def allocate_backorders(orders: Sequence[Tuple[str, int, int, Mapping[str, int]]], available: Mapping[str, int]) -> Dict[str, Dict[str, int]]:
functions.summary: Allocate available stock to open backorders by priority
functions.spec:
Allocate available stock to open customer backorders.

Args:
    orders: (order_id, priority, order_day, lines) tuples, where lines maps
        SKU -> backordered eaches. Priority 1 is the most urgent; larger
        numbers are less urgent.
    available: SKU -> eaches available to promise. SKUs that are missing
        have 0 available.

Orders are served one after another in this sequence: priority ascending,
then order_day ascending, then order_id ascending. Stock handed to one
order is no longer available to the orders after it.

Returns:
    Dict order_id -> {sku: allocated eaches} with an entry for every order and
    every SKU on its lines (0 where nothing was allocated). The inputs are not
    modified.

Raises:
    ValueError: on a duplicate order_id or a line qty <= 0.

Example:
    allocate_backorders([("o1", 2, 10, {"S": 5}), ("o2", 1, 12, {"S": 4})], {"S": 4})
        == {"o1": {"S": 0}, "o2": {"S": 4}}
functions.clarification:
Backorders ship complete; we never send a customer part of a backorder. An
order is allocated all of its lines in full or nothing at all. An order that
does not fit in what is left gets 0 on every line and leaves the stock untouched,
and allocation continues with the next order in the sequence (a smaller order
further down may still be filled).

functions.signature: def stock_valuation(on_hand: Mapping[str, int], cost_layers: Mapping[str, Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]]) -> Tuple[List[Tuple[str, int, int, int]], int]:
functions.summary: Build the stock valuation report at weighted average cost
functions.spec:
Value on-hand stock at weighted average cost.

Args:
    on_hand: SKU -> eaches on hand. Keys may be in any format accepted by
        normalize_sku; quantities of keys that normalize to the same SKU are
        added together.
    cost_layers: canonical SKU -> list of (qty, unit_cost_cents) layers,
        averaged with weighted_average_cost.

Returns:
    (rows, total_cents). rows is a list of (sku, qty, unit_cost_cents,
    value_cents) with value = qty * unit cost, sorted by value descending,
    then SKU ascending; total_cents is the sum of the row values.

Raises:
    KeyError: if a SKU that has to be valued has no entry in cost_layers.
    ValueError: from normalize_sku or weighted_average_cost.

Example:
    stock_valuation({"abc-123456-1": 10}, {"ABC-123456-1": [(5, 200), (5, 300)]})
        == ([("ABC-123456-1", 10, 250, 2500)], 2500)
functions.clarification:
Only positive stock is valued. SKUs whose (combined) on-hand is zero or
negative are left out of the rows and the total entirely (negative stock must
not reduce the reported value), and they do not need cost layers.

functions.signature: def parse_movement_line(line: str, case_sizes: Mapping[str, int]) -> Dict[str, Any]:
functions.summary: Parse a stock movement record into a normalized dict
functions.spec:
Parse one stock movement record.

Records are semicolon-separated: "<day>;<type>;<sku>;<location>;<quantity>",
e.g. "12;RCV;ABC-123456-1;B-07-14-3;5 CS". Whitespace around fields is ignored.

    day       non-negative integer day index
    type      RCV (receipt), SHP (shipment), RTN (customer return) or
              ADJ (inventory adjustment); case-insensitive
    sku       normalized with normalize_sku
    location  parsed with parse_location
    quantity  parsed with parse_quantity, using case_sizes[sku]; SKUs that
              are not in case_sizes have a case size of 1

Returns:
    {"day": int, "type": str, "sku": str, "location": str, "qty": int}
    where type is upper-case, sku is canonical, location is the canonical
    "Z-AA-SS-L" string (two-digit aisle and shelf) and qty is the signed
    change to on-hand stock in eaches: RCV and RTN add stock, SHP removes it
    (the record shows the shipped amount, qty is its negative), ADJ is
    applied as written.

Raises:
    ValueError: wrong number of fields, bad day, unknown type, or any error
        raised by the helpers above.

Example:
    parse_movement_line("12;SHP;abc-123456-1;b-07-14-3;2 CS", {"ABC-123456-1": 6})
        == {"day": 12, "type": "SHP", "sku": "ABC-123456-1",
            "location": "B-07-14-3", "qty": -12}
functions.clarification:
Only ADJ records may carry a sign. RCV, SHP and RTN quantities must be
strictly positive as written; a zero or negative quantity on those types is a
data-entry error and raises ValueError (a negative SHP is NOT a return; returns
are booked as RTN). A zero ADJ is rejected as well.

functions.signature: def on_hand_by_location(lines: Iterable[str], case_sizes: Mapping[str, int], as_of_day: Optional[int] = None) -> Dict[Tuple[str, str], int]:
functions.summary: Compute on-hand stock per SKU and bin location from movement records
functions.spec:
Current on-hand stock per (SKU, location) from movement records.

Each line is parsed with parse_movement_line, except blank lines and
comment lines (first non-blank character "#"), which are skipped. The signed
quantities are summed per (sku, location), using the canonical SKU and
location strings returned by the parser.

Args:
    lines: movement records (see parse_movement_line).
    case_sizes: passed through to parse_movement_line.
    as_of_day: if given, only movements with day <= as_of_day are counted.

Returns:
    Dict (sku, location) -> eaches on hand.

Raises:
    ValueError: propagated from parse_movement_line for malformed records.

Example:
    on_hand_by_location(["1;RCV;ABC-123456-1;B-07-14-3;10 EA",
                         "2;SHP;ABC-123456-1;B-07-14-3;4 EA"], {})
        == {("ABC-123456-1", "B-07-14-3"): 6}
functions.clarification:
Positions that net to exactly zero are dropped from the result: an emptied
bin is not a stock position and must not show up on count sheets or transfer
screens. Negative totals are kept as they are (they flag a missed receipt and
must stay visible).

functions.signature: def average_daily_demand(lines: Iterable[str], case_sizes: Mapping[str, int], sku: str, start_day: int, end_day: int) -> int:
functions.summary: Compute a SKU's average daily demand over a day range
functions.spec:
Average daily demand for one SKU over a range of days, in whole eaches.

Movement records are parsed with parse_movement_line (blank lines and "#"
comment lines are skipped). Shipments (SHP) of `sku` dated start_day ..
end_day (both inclusive) are totalled and divided by the number of days in
the range; the result is rounded up to a whole each.

Args:
    lines: movement records.
    case_sizes: passed through to parse_movement_line.
    sku: canonical SKU.
    start_day, end_day: inclusive day range.

Raises:
    ValueError: if end_day < start_day, or for malformed records.

Example:
    lines = ["1;SHP;ABC-123456-1;B-07-14-3;7 EA", "2;SHP;ABC-123456-1;A-01-01-1;3 EA"]
    average_daily_demand(lines, {}, "ABC-123456-1", 1, 4) == 3     # 10 / 4 = 2.5 -> 3
functions.clarification:
Demand is net of customer returns: RTN records of the SKU in the same day
range are subtracted from the shipped total before averaging. If returns exceed
shipments the demand is 0, never negative.

functions.signature: def dead_stock(lines: Iterable[str], case_sizes: Mapping[str, int], today: int, idle_days: int) -> List[str]:
functions.summary: Find SKUs with stock on hand that have not shipped for a long time
functions.spec:
List SKUs whose stock has not moved out for a long time (dead stock).

A SKU is dead stock when its total on-hand (summed over all locations with
on_hand_by_location, counting movements up to and including `today`) is
positive and its most recent shipment (SHP) is at least `idle_days` days old,
i.e. today - last_ship_day >= idle_days. Movements dated after `today` are
ignored. Blank lines and "#" comment lines are skipped.

Args:
    lines: movement records; any iterable (it is only iterated once).
    case_sizes: passed through to the parsers.
    today: current day index.
    idle_days: threshold in days, >= 1.

Returns:
    Sorted list of canonical SKUs.

Raises:
    ValueError: if idle_days < 1, or for malformed records.

Example:
    lines = ["1;RCV;ABC-123456-1;B-07-14-3;10 EA", "5;SHP;ABC-123456-1;B-07-14-3;2 EA"]
    dead_stock(lines, {}, today=40, idle_days=30) == ["ABC-123456-1"]
functions.clarification:
A SKU that has never shipped (as of today) is measured from its earliest
movement of any type instead, normally its first receipt: a product that
arrived last week is new, not dead.

functions.signature: def cycle_count_variance(lines: Iterable[str], case_sizes: Mapping[str, int], counts: Mapping[Tuple[str, str], int]) -> List[Tuple[str, str, int]]:
functions.summary: Report differences between a cycle count and system stock
functions.spec:
Compare a cycle count with system stock and report the differences.

System stock is on_hand_by_location(lines, case_sizes). `counts` holds what
the counters recorded, keyed by (sku, location) as typed on the handheld;
keys are normalized with normalize_sku and parse_location (canonical
"Z-AA-SS-L" location string) before matching, and the quantities of keys
that normalize to the same position are added together.

    variance = counted qty - system qty

Returns:
    List of (sku, location, variance) for every position with a non-zero
    variance, sorted by location, then SKU.

Raises:
    ValueError: if a counted quantity is negative, or from the parsers.

Example:
    lines = ["1;RCV;ABC-123456-1;B-07-14-3;10 EA"]
    cycle_count_variance(lines, {}, {("abc-123456-1", "b-07-14-3"): 8})
        == [("ABC-123456-1", "B-07-14-3", -2)]
functions.clarification:
A count covers the whole bin. If a location appears in `counts`, every system
position in that location whose SKU was not counted is treated as counted 0
(variance = -system qty). Locations that were not counted at all are ignored,
even if they hold stock.

functions.signature: def validate_transfer(lines: Iterable[str], case_sizes: Mapping[str, int], sku: str, from_location: str, to_location: str, qty: int, day: int) -> List[str]:
functions.summary: Validate a bin-to-bin stock transfer and list the problems
functions.spec:
Check a proposed bin-to-bin transfer and list what is wrong with it.

Args:
    lines: movement records used to work out stock (see on_hand_by_location).
    case_sizes: passed through to the parsers.
    sku: canonical SKU to move.
    from_location, to_location: location codes, parsed with parse_location
        (a malformed code raises ValueError).
    qty: eaches to move.
    day: day index the transfer is executed on.

Returns:
    List of problem codes in this order, empty if the transfer is fine:
        "BAD_QTY"             qty <= 0
        "SAME_LOCATION"       both codes refer to the same bin
        "INSUFFICIENT_STOCK"  qty > 0 and the SKU's on-hand at from_location
                              is less than qty (no position counts as 0)

Example:
    lines = ["1;RCV;ABC-123456-1;B-07-14-3;10 EA"]
    validate_transfer(lines, {}, "ABC-123456-1", "B-07-14-3", "b-07-14-3", 0, day=2)
        == ["BAD_QTY", "SAME_LOCATION"]
functions.clarification:
Movements are posted overnight: records dated on the transfer day itself are
not in the books yet and must not count toward the available stock. Only
movements with day < `day` count.

functions.signature: def pick_route_order(picks: Sequence[Tuple[str, str, int]]) -> List[Tuple[str, str, int]]:
functions.summary: Sort pick lines into the picker's walking order
functions.spec:
Order pick lines along the picker's walking route.

Args:
    picks: (sku, location, qty) tuples; locations are parsed with
        parse_location (a malformed code raises ValueError).

Returns:
    The same tuples, unchanged, reordered for walking: by zone
    (alphabetical), then aisle (ascending), then by shelf position along the
    aisle, then level (ascending). Picks at the same bin keep their input
    order.

Example:
    pick_route_order([("S2", "A-01-05-1", 1), ("S1", "A-01-02-1", 3)])
        == [("S1", "A-01-02-1", 3), ("S2", "A-01-05-1", 1)]
functions.clarification:
Pickers walk the aisles in a serpentine (S-shaped) path: up the odd-numbered
aisles and back down the even-numbered ones. Shelves are therefore visited in
ascending order in odd aisles and in DESCENDING order in even aisles. Levels
within a shelf are always ascending.

functions.signature: def replenishment_suggestions(items: Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]]) -> List[Tuple[str, int]]:
functions.summary: Suggest purchase orders for SKUs at or below their reorder point
functions.spec:
Suggest purchase orders for SKUs that have reached their reorder point.

Each item is a mapping with the keys
    "sku", "on_hand", "on_order"          SKU string and ints
    "daily_demand", "lead_times"          histories for reorder_point
    "review_period_days"                  optional, default 0
    "annual_demand", "order_cost_cents",
    "holding_cost_cents", "pack_size"     inputs for economic_order_quantity

Inventory position = on_hand + on_order. An item needs a purchase order when
its inventory position is at or below its reorder point
(reorder_point(daily_demand, lead_times, review_period_days)). The suggested
quantity is based on the item's economic order quantity.

Returns:
    List of (sku, qty) for the items that need ordering, sorted by SKU.

Example:
    item = {"sku": "ABC-123456-1", "on_hand": 50, "on_order": 0,
            "daily_demand": [10, 10], "lead_times": [5],
            "annual_demand": 3650, "order_cost_cents": 1000,
            "holding_cost_cents": 200, "pack_size": 10}
    replenishment_suggestions([item]) == [("ABC-123456-1", 190)]
functions.clarification:
The EOQ is a floor, not a fixed amount: if inventory position + EOQ would
still be at or below the reorder point, order instead the smallest number of
whole packs (rounded UP, not with round_to_pack) that lifts the inventory
position above the reorder point.
